items.stem: Describe Oldham and Brass’s (1979) study.
items.answer: A quasi-experiment at a US newspaper office measured employees’ satisfaction and motivation before and after a move from conventional offices to an open-plan office, with control groups. After the move, satisfaction with work and supervisors, friendship opportunities and internal motivation fell, and employees reported more interruptions and less concentration.

items.answer: The novelty and attention could cause a temporary Hawthorne effect, so long-term measures are needed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark Hawthorne/novelty; 1 mark need for later measure [2]

items.stem: A technology company in Doha plans to move all staff into one open-plan office to save money and improve teamwork. (a) Suggest two ways the company could reduce the problems of open-plan offices. (b) Explain why measuring staff satisfaction straight after the move might be misleading.
items.answer: (a) Provide quiet rooms or booths for concentration, use partitions or sound-absorbing materials, and allow some home working. (b) The novelty and attention could cause a temporary Hawthorne effect, so long-term measures are needed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark Hawthorne/novelty; 1 mark need for later measure [2]

items.stem: Evaluate Oldham and Brass’s (1979) study of a move to an open-plan office in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about self-report.
items.answer: Strength (controls): Measures before and after the move, plus control groups, allowed change to be attributed to the office design. Strength (ecological validity): It was a real office move with real employees, so the findings reflect real working life. Weakness (generalisability): It studied one newspaper organisation, so the findings may not apply to other types of work. Weakness (self-report): Satisfaction was measured by questionnaire, which may be affected by social desirability. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: “Fox et al.’s (1987) token economy for safety in mines has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including reporting bias in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (ecological validity): It was carried out in real mines over many years with real injury records. Strength (usefulness): Large reductions in injuries and costs show that behavioural safety programmes can work. Weakness (controls): With no control mine, other changes such as new equipment might explain the improvement. Weakness (reporting bias): Workers may have hidden minor injuries to keep their stamps. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “Features of the work environment such as lighting, noise, temperature and space”?
items.answer: Physical work conditions
items.markingKey: Physical work conditions: features of the work environment such as lighting, noise, temperature and space. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “The Hawthorne effect is a problem for studies of work conditions.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe Oldham and Brass’s (1979) study.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Workers may change behaviour because they know they are being studied. (b) A quasi-experiment at a US newspaper office measured employees’ satisfaction and motivation before and after a move from conventional offices to an open-plan office, with control groups. After the move, satisfaction with work and supervisors, friendship opportunities and internal motivation fell, and employees reported more interruptions and less concentration.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark design; 1 mark measures; 1 mark findings [3]

items.stem: With reference to Oldham and Brass’s (1979) study of a move to an open-plan office, explain one strength relating to controls.
items.answer: Measures before and after the move, plus control groups, allowed change to be attributed to the office design.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to controls; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A technology company in Bogotá plans to move all staff into one open-plan office to save money and improve teamwork. Using research, explain one risk of this change.
items.answer: Oldham and Brass found satisfaction and internal motivation fell after a move to open-plan, partly due to interruptions and lack of privacy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark risk; 1 mark research [2]

items.stem: Kenji measured the number of errors made in a data-entry task by 7 employees in Colombo working in a quiet private office and 7 employees in a noisy open-plan office. Table: Errors per hour — Private office: 11, 14, 10, 12, 10, 7, 12. Open-plan office: 13, 23, 13, 15, 13, 10, 17. Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place.
items.answer: Private office: 10.9; open-plan office: 14.9.
items.markingKey: Private office: 76 ÷ 7 = 10.9; open-plan office: 104 ÷ 7 = 14.9. 1 mark for each correct mean [2]

items.stem: A company in Bogotá compared data-entry errors per hour for 7 staff in private offices and 7 staff in an open-plan office. Table: Errors per hour — Private office: 15, 12, 12, 10, 11, 14, 14. Open-plan office: 17, 19, 23, 22, 21, 23, 20. (a) Calculate the median score for the private office condition. (b) The standard deviation for the private office condition was 1.81 and for the open-plan office condition was 2.21. Explain what these values show.
items.answer: (a) 12 (b) The open-plan office condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent.
items.markingKey: (a) Ordered scores: 10, 11, 12, 12, 14, 14, 15; median = 12. 1 mark: data ordered; 1 mark: correct median [2] (b) 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2]

items.stem: Design a questionnaire to investigate how employees feel about moving to an open-plan office. Your plan must include: how the data will be analysed, one example question and ethical issues.
items.answer: Method: a questionnaire. Closed questions (for example rating scales from 1 to 5) for quantitative data and at least one open question for qualitative detail; pilot the questions; avoid leading questions. Variables: theme 1: privacy; theme 2: communication with colleagues. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Hanoi, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: ‘Organisations can reduce the harmful effects of shift work.’ Discuss this view. In your answer, you may refer to individual differences and biological explanations.
items.answer: Arguments for: Czeisler et al. (1982) found forward rotation and longer rotation periods improved satisfaction, health and productivity. Bright light and planned sleep can help adjust circadian rhythms. Arguments against: Gold et al. (1992) found rotating nurses had more sleep problems and accidents than fixed-shift nurses. Some workers never fully adjust to nights, and family life is disrupted. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “A shift system in which workers change shift every few days”.
items.answer: Rapid rotation
items.markingKey: Rapid rotation: a shift system in which workers change shift every few days. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “Rotating shift workers may be at greater risk of accidents than fixed-shift workers.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe the findings of Czeisler et al. (1982).
items.answer: (a) Correct. Gold et al. found nurses on rotating shifts reported more accidents and errors. (b) Workers moved from backward rotation every week to forward rotation (some with 21-day rotation) reported greater satisfaction with their schedules and better health; staff turnover fell and productivity rose.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark change made; 2 marks findings [3]

items.stem: With reference to Czeisler et al.’s (1982) study of shift rotation, explain one weakness relating to generalisability.
items.answer: It studied one male-dominated industrial plant, so the results may not apply to other jobs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to generalisability; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A hospital in Bogotá asked nurses on different schedules whether they had nodded off while driving to or from work in the past year. Rotating shifts: yes 31, no 79; Fixed day shift: yes 11, no 94. Calculate the percentage of nurses for Rotating shifts that were “yes”. Give your answer to one decimal place.

Jonas measured the number of errors made in a data-entry task by 6 employees in Jakarta working in a quiet private office and 6 employees in a noisy open-plan office. Table: Errors per hour — Private office: 11, 9, 6, 11, 11, 5. Open-plan office: 8, 13, 12, 13, 12, 12. Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place.
items.answer: Private office: 8.8; open-plan office: 11.7.
items.markingKey: Private office: 53 ÷ 6 = 8.8; open-plan office: 70 ÷ 6 = 11.7. 1 mark for each correct mean [2]

items.stem: A factory in Cape Town rotates workers every week from nights to afternoons to mornings. Accidents are highest in the first days after each change. (a) Using research, suggest two changes to the schedule. (b) Explain why accidents are highest just after a change.
items.answer: (a) Rotate forwards (morning → afternoon → night) and lengthen the rotation period, for example to 21 days (Czeisler et al.). (b) Circadian rhythms have not adjusted to the new hours, so workers are sleepy and less alert.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark rhythm; 1 mark alertness [2]

items.stem: Define the term ‘lapse’.
items.answer: In Reason’s classification, a memory failure, such as forgetting a step.
items.markingKey: Lapse: in Reason’s classification, a memory failure, such as forgetting a step. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: In a revision session, a student says: “A token economy can be used to promote workplace safety.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Fox et al. (1987) rewarded injury-free periods with stamps.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Fox et al.’s (1987) token economy for safety in mines can be evaluated in terms of controls. Explain one weakness of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: With no control mine, other changes such as new equipment might explain the improvement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to controls; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Leila measured the number of errors made in a data-entry task by 8 employees in Madrid working in a quiet private office and 8 employees in a noisy open-plan office. Table: Errors per hour — Private office: 14, 6, 14, 6, 13, 8, 10, 7. Open-plan office: 17, 15, 15, 15, 13, 17, 6, 13. Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study.
items.answer: IV: the type of office (private or open-plan). DV: the number of data-entry errors per hour recorded by the computer system.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that open-plan offices are good for employees? In your answer, you may refer to usefulness and individual differences.
items.answer: Arguments for: They can increase communication and teamwork and make supervisors more accessible. They are cheaper and more flexible. Arguments against: Oldham and Brass (1979) found satisfaction and motivation fell after a move to open-plan. Noise and interruptions reduce concentration and privacy. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
